rationale: A wins because it treats the missing economics as the story, not an inconvenience: "Brands get paid on day one. Who carries the 60-day float?" is exactly the question a real reporter asks. B has usable bones, but "Faire is quietly becoming a lender to 700,000 small retailers" turns marketplace size into borrower eligibility, and "crossing into balance-sheet finance" states what the update does not prove. That is not a sharper angle; it is an avoidable fact-check wound.
gaps_in_A: "rather than a bank score" is an unsupported contrast. The update says Faire uses order history; it does not say what credit signal Faire is replacing.
"cash flow, not demand" overstates the evidence. "Top barrier" does not prove demand is not also a barrier.
The set is strong, but two kept angles still die without named sources: "one named retailer" and "one brand willing to say" are not nice-to-haves here.
gaps_in_B: "to 700,000 small retailers" is the big sin. The 700,000 figure is marketplace size, not disclosed eligibility or credit access.
"That's a marketplace crossing into balance-sheet finance" invents funding exposure while the same angle admits it still needs to know whether the credit sits on Faire's balance sheet or a partner's.
"Small brands on Faire now get paid before the retailer pays" adds "small" and implies a new payment-status change the update does not establish.
"using order history instead of traditional credit files" is another unsupported contrast. Order-history underwriting is in the update; displacement of traditional credit files is not.
